Summary

On December 8, 1987, an Israeli army truck collided with civilian vehicles at the Erez checkpoint in Gaza, killing four Palestinian workers from Jabalia refugee camp. Palestinians believed it was deliberate revenge for the stabbing death of an Israeli in Gaza two days earlier. The following day, December 9, massive protests erupted in Jabalia. When 17-year-old Hatem al-Sisi was shot dead by Israeli soldiers, the uprising exploded across Gaza, East Jerusalem, and the West Bank within days. What began as spontaneous protests transformed into organized, sustained civil resistance coordinated by grassroots committees and later by the United National Leadership of the Uprising (UNLU).

The Intifada was characterized by largely non-violent tactics: general strikes, tax resistance, boycotts of Israeli products, and civil disobedience. Palestinian youth confronted Israeli soldiers with stones and Molotov cocktails. The Israeli response was brutal. Defense Minister Yitzhak Rabin issued orders to use 'force, might, and beatings' and to 'break bones' of demonstrators. Soldiers systematically beat protesters, fired live ammunition at stone-throwers, and used tear gas extensively. In the first year alone, Israeli forces killed at least 300 Palestinians and wounded tens of thousands. By 1990, the death toll exceeded 1,000.

The uprising exacted an enormous toll: 1,087-1,284 Palestinians killed (including 241-332 children), over 120,000 wounded, approximately 20,000 arrested in the first year alone (with estimates reaching 120,000 total over six years), 2,532 homes demolished, and 481 Palestinians deported. Approximately 160-200 Israelis (soldiers and civilians) were killed during the same period. International condemnation was swift—the UN Security Council condemned Israel's response, and even the Reagan Administration criticized the 'harsh security measures and excessive use of live ammunition.' The Intifada forced recognition of Palestinian national aspirations, led to the Madrid Conference (1991) and secret Oslo negotiations, culminating in the September 1993 Oslo Accords which created the Palestinian Authority and promised future statehood—though these promises remain unfulfilled over 30 years later.

Timeline

1987-12-08 00:00:00
Trigger: Traffic accident in Gaza
Israeli army truck collides with civilian vehicles at Erez checkpoint, killing four Palestinian workers from Jabalia refugee camp (Gaza). Palestinians believe it was deliberate revenge for Israeli stabbing two days earlier. Rumors and anger spread rapidly.
Al Jazeera - First Intifada History; Britannica - Intifada
1987-12-09 00:00:00
Intifada begins: Jabalia uprising
Mass protests erupt in Jabalia refugee camp. 17-year-old Hatem al-Sisi shot dead by Israeli soldier after throwing Molotov cocktail at army patrol. His death becomes symbol. Protests spread throughout Gaza Strip within hours.
PalQuest - First Intifada 1987-1993
10-15 December 1987
Uprising spreads to West Bank and Jerusalem
Protests expand to East Jerusalem, Ramallah, Nablus, Hebron, and other West Bank cities and refugee camps. Rock-throwing, tire burning, roadblocks become daily occurrences. Six Palestinians killed, 30 injured in first week.
Jewish Virtual Library - First Intifada
1988-01-01 00:00:00
Rabin's 'Iron Fist' policy announced
Defense Minister Yitzhak Rabin declares policy of 'force, might, and beatings.' Orders soldiers to 'break bones' of stone-throwers. Israeli forces begin systematic beatings with clubs and rifle butts. At least 300 Palestinians killed in first year.
PalQuest Documentation

Formation of United National Leadership (UNLU)
Underground coordination committee forms comprising PLO factions and local leaders. Begin issuing communiqués (bayanat) directing strikes, boycotts, demonstrations. Organize parallel institutions: popular committees, alternative education, medical relief.
PalQuest - First Intifada
December 1987 - December 1988
First year: Peak violence
First year death toll: at least 300 Palestinians killed, tens of thousands wounded. Over 18,000 arrested. Israeli forces close schools and universities, impose curfews, demolish homes. 3,600+ Molotov cocktail attacks, 100 hand grenade attacks reported.
War Wings Daily - First Intifada Analysis
1988-11-15 00:00:00
Palestinian Declaration of Independence
Palestine National Council in Algiers declares Palestinian statehood. PLO recognizes Israel's right to exist, accepts UN Resolutions 242 and 338, adopts two-state solution. Authored by Mahmoud Darwish. Major political shift driven by Intifada momentum.
PalQuest - Declaration Context
1990-10-08 00:00:00
Temple Mount Massacre
Israeli police kill 22 Palestinians at Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in Jerusalem during prayers. Hundreds wounded. Incident marks shift toward more lethal Palestinian tactics. Three Israelis and one IDF soldier stabbed to death in Jerusalem and Gaza two weeks later.
Historical Records
1990-1991
Violence escalates; 'Intrafada' begins
Palestinian armed attacks increase. Hamas challenges PLO leadership. 'Intrafada': Palestinians kill other Palestinians accused of collaboration with Israel. By 1991, number killed by Palestinian death squads exceeds those killed by Israeli forces in some periods.
Jewish Virtual Library Documentation
1991-10-30 00:00:00
Madrid Peace Conference
First direct Israeli-Palestinian negotiations. Palestinians represented by delegation from occupied territories (not PLO formally). Grassroots activists and women leaders prominent in delegation. Conference marks international recognition of Palestinian rights.
PBS - Intifada Impact
1992-1993
Secret Oslo negotiations
While Madrid talks stall, secret back-channel negotiations begin in Oslo, Norway between Israel and PLO. Grassroots leaders and women excluded from Oslo process, unlike Madrid. Negotiations produce framework for Palestinian self-government.
PBS Documentation
1993-09-13 00:00:00
Oslo Accords signed; Intifada ends
Israel and PLO sign Declaration of Principles on White House lawn. Agreement provides framework for Palestinian self-government, Israeli withdrawal from some territories, creation of Palestinian Authority. Intifada officially ends after nearly six years. Final toll: 1,087-1,284 Palestinians killed, 160-200 Israelis killed.

Testimony

Yitzhak Rabin
“Issued notorious orders to soldiers: 'The first priority is to use force, might, and beatings.' Later told officers: 'Break their bones.' Admitted policy in interview: 'I told the army to go in and use force, to beat up the demonstrators.' Later as Prime Minister (1992-1995), pursued peace negotiations that grew from Intifada.”
Contemporary interviews and military records; documented by Israeli media
Mahmoud Darwish
“Authored 1988 Palestinian Declaration of Independence. Wrote: 'Because of the Intifada and its revolutionary and irreversible impulse, the history of Palestine has therefore arrived at a decisive juncture.' Described Intifada as transformative moment for Palestinian national movement.”
Palestinian Declaration of Independence (1988); interviews
United Nations
“Security Council condemned Israeli practices multiple times. Resolutions 607 and 608 (1988) condemned deportations. Human Rights investigators documented: 'The Israeli military response has been characterized by excessive and indiscriminate use of force against Palestinian civilians, including children.'”
UN Security Council Resolutions 607, 608; UN Human Rights reports
Amnesty International
“Documented systematic torture in Israeli detention centers. Report stated: 'Palestinians detained during the Intifada have been subjected to torture and ill-treatment systematically and on a wide scale.' Described beatings, stress positions, sleep deprivation, threats as routine.”
Amnesty International reports (1988-1993)
B'Tselem (Israeli human rights org)
“Founded during Intifada (1989) to document violations. Comprehensive statistics: 1,087 Palestinians killed (including 241 children), 120,000+ wounded, 2,532 homes demolished, 481 deported. Stated: 'Israeli forces systematically violated international humanitarian law during the Intifada.'”
B'Tselem statistical reports and documentation
Palestinian Youth Activist
“Interviewed for Al Jazeera documentary: 'We refused to give Israel money to build a more powerful army to oppress Palestinians. The Israeli army besieged our city for 40 days. They raided or demolished homes of those who withheld tax. We saw new types of injuries—first from tear gas and rubber bullets, then from beatings and real bullets.'”

“Reflected on Intifada: 'The Palestinians' nonviolent resistance in the First Intifada was a remarkable demonstration of courage. War crimes

Excessive Use of Lethal Force
Israeli forces routinely used live ammunition against stone-throwing demonstrators, killing over 1,000 Palestinians. UN criticized Israel's shoot-to-kill policies. Many victims shot in upper body/head, indicating lethal intent. Use of force disproportionate to threat posed by largely unarmed protesters.
📄 B'Tselem Documentation →
Systematic Beatings and Bone-Breaking Policy
Defense Minister Rabin's explicit orders to 'break bones' of protesters. Soldiers systematically beat Palestinians with clubs and rifle butts. At least 17 Palestinians died from beatings alone. Thousands suffered broken bones, permanent injuries. Policy constituted torture and cruel, inhuman treatment prohibited under international law.
📄 PalQuest Documentation →
Punitive Home Demolitions
2,532 Palestinian homes demolished during Intifada as collective punishment—homes of families of suspected attackers or activists demolished without trial. Violates Fourth Geneva Convention Article 33: 'Collective penalties...are prohibited.' Thousands rendered homeless.
📄 B'Tselem Reports →
Mass Arbitrary Detention and Torture
Approximately 120,000 Palestinians arrested over six years—roughly 20% of adult male population. Many held in administrative detention without charge or trial. Widespread torture documented by human rights organizations. Detention centers described as torture facilities.
📄 Human Rights Documentation →
Collective Punishment
Extended curfews affecting entire towns and refugee camps for weeks. Closures of schools and universities for months/years, denying education to entire generation. Sealing of entire areas. All constitute collective punishment prohibited under Geneva Convention Article 33.
📄 B'Tselem Reports →
Illegal Deportations
481 Palestinians deported from occupied territories to Lebanon and elsewhere—direct violation of Fourth Geneva Convention Article 49: 'Individual or mass forcible transfers...from occupied territory...are prohibited.' UN Security Council Resolutions 607 and 608 condemned deportations.
📄 UN Resolutions →
Killing of Children
241-332 Palestinian children (minors under 18) killed by Israeli forces during Intifada. Many shot while throwing stones or participating in protests. International outcry over images of soldiers shooting children. Killing of children disproportionate and violated principles of distinction and proportionality.
📄 B'Tselem Statistics →

Legal classification

Fourth Geneva Convention - Violations
<strong>Article 33:</strong> 'No protected person may be punished for an offence he or she has not personally committed. Collective penalties...are prohibited.' Home demolitions and collective curfews violated this provision.
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
<strong>Article 6 (Right to Life):</strong> Use of lethal force against largely unarmed protesters violated right to life. Force used was not strictly necessary or proportionate.
UN Security Council Resolutions
<strong>Resolutions 607 (1988) and 608 (1988):</strong> Condemned Israel's deportation of Palestinian civilians. Demanded Israel cease deportations and allow deportees to return. Israel rejected resolutions.
International Criticism and Condemnation
<strong>UN Human Rights Council:</strong> Multiple fact-finding missions documented violations. Special Rapporteur reports detailed systematic abuses.
Fourth Geneva Convention - Violations
<strong>Article 49:</strong> 'Individual or mass forcible transfers...are prohibited.' 481 deportations directly violated this protection.
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
<strong>Article 7 (Prohibition of Torture):</strong> Systematic beatings, bone-breaking policy, and torture in detention centers violated absolute prohibition on torture and cruel, inhuman treatment.
UN Security Council Resolutions
<strong>Multiple resolutions:</strong> Security Council passed numerous resolutions condemning Israeli practices during Intifada, including excessive use of force, collective punishment, and violations of Palestinian rights.
International Criticism and Condemnation
<strong>US State Department:</strong> Even US government (Israel's closest ally) condemned 'harsh security measures and excessive use of live ammunition' under Reagan Administration.
Fourth Geneva Convention - Violations
<strong>Article 147 (Grave Breaches):</strong> 'Willful killing...torture or inhuman treatment...extensive destruction...not justified by military necessity' constitute war crimes. Bone-breaking policy and excessive force qualify as grave breaches.
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
<strong>Article 9 (Liberty and Security):</strong> Mass arbitrary detentions, administrative detention without charge violated right to liberty and protection from arbitrary arrest.
International Criticism and Condemnation
<strong>Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch:</strong> Both organizations issued reports documenting torture, arbitrary detention, excessive force, and other violations.
International Criticism and Condemnation
<strong>International Committee of the Red Cross:</strong> Repeatedly raised concerns about treatment of detainees and use of force against civilians.

Commanders

Yitzhak Rabin Israeli Defense Minister (1984-1990); Prime Minister (1992-1995)
Issued 'iron fist' orders including bone-breaking policy. Later acknowledged brutality excessive. As PM, pursued Oslo peace process that emerged from Intifada. Assassinated by Israeli extremist in 1995.
Yasser Arafat PLO Chairman
Led PLO from exile. Initially caught off-guard by grassroots uprising, later asserted control. Authorized 1988 Declaration of Independence. Led Oslo negotiations resulting in 1993 accords.
Hanan Ashrawi Palestinian spokeswoman; academic
Prominent spokesperson for Palestinian cause during Intifada. Articulated Palestinian aspirations to international media. Key figure in Madrid Conference delegation. Later Palestinian legislator.
United National Leadership of Uprising (UNLU) Underground coordinating committee
Coordinated strikes, boycotts, demonstrations through communiqués. Comprised representatives of PLO factions and grassroots leaders. Organized parallel institutions and civil disobedience campaigns.
